scenario: After a Friday release, customers get a blank page. Front Door has been holding index.html for 24 hours, and it points at hashed bundles the deploy removed.
stem: Which change fixes this for future releases?
options: Keep the 24-hour rule and purge every path at the end of each deployment pipeline run
Turn off Front Door caching for the whole site so that nothing can ever be served stale
no-cache for index.html; a year and immutable for hashed assets
Add a ?v= query string to index.html and keep caching it at the edge for a day
explanation: The HTML is the one file that must always be checked, and hashed files can be kept for a year because their names change with their content. Purging on every deploy hides the wrong policy, takes up to ten minutes and still fails tabs already open, while turning caching off throws away the edge for files that are safe to cache.

stem: Front Door's route has caching enabled with 'honour origin', and a Node endpoint returns a response with no Cache-Control or Expires header. What does Front Door do?
options: Caches it for a random duration between one and three days
Doesn't cache it, because the origin gave no instruction
Caches it for exactly 24 hours, the documented default
Caches it until someone purges the path
explanation: Microsoft documents that without a Cache-Control header Front Door picks a duration between one and three days. That is why a forgotten header is dangerous: 'no instruction' doesn't mean 'don't cache'. Always send an explicit header from every endpoint.

scenario: To survive a flash sale, someone adds Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 to /api/home, which greets the signed-in shopper by name. The app sends a bearer token in the Authorization header.
stem: Why did other shoppers see one customer's name?
options: Front Door always ignores the Authorization header and caches every GET request it sees
The WAF stored the response while inspecting it and then replayed it to other shoppers
Front Door includes the session cookie in the cache key, and that cookie had expired
public allowed caching, and the cache key is the path, not the user
explanation: Front Door doesn't normally cache requests that carry an Authorization header, but a response marked public, s-maxage or must-revalidate overrides that. Because the cache key is built from the path and query string, never the token or cookie, every shopper asking for /api/home got the same copy. Personal responses must send private, no-store.

scenario: Ana adds a route rule for /index.html with Cache-Control: no-cache, but a deep link like /orders/4821 still comes back without that header.
stem: Where should the HTML cache policy go instead?
options: In a second route rule for /orders/*
In globalHeaders, because route rules are not applied to requests answered by the navigation fallback
In a meta http-equiv tag inside index.html
Only in a Front Door rule set, because Static Web Apps can't set Cache-Control
explanation: Requests that trigger navigationFallback skip route rules, so deep links only get globalHeaders. Setting no-cache globally and overriding it for /assets/* covers every HTML response. A meta tag is ignored by Front Door and other shared caches, and Static Web Apps can set headers itself.

scenario: A team's React app runs on Static Web Apps Standard. They need managed WAF rules, a rate limit on /login, and one entry point that also routes /api to API Management.
options: Enterprise-grade edge, because it is Azure Front Door run and configured for you
Static Web Apps on its own, because it already serves files from a global edge
Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) in front of the Static Web Apps origin
Their own Front Door Premium profile, with Static Web Apps as an origin
explanation: Enterprise-grade edge needs no configuration, but it doesn't let you add a WAF or your own routing rules. A manual Front Door profile does, and Premium adds the managed WAF rule sets. Azure CDN classic accepts no new profiles and retires in September 2027.

stem: Which statement about cache purge in Front Door Standard and Premium is correct?
options: It takes up to ten minutes to propagate, so keep it for emergencies
It is instant and free, so the recommended practice is to purge every path on each deployment
It purges only the exact URL, so every query-string variation must be listed separately
It is available only on the Premium tier
explanation: Purges propagate over minutes, and Microsoft recommends versioning assets at new URLs rather than relying on purge. Purge is case-insensitive and ignores the query string, so one path clears all its variations, and it is available on both Standard and Premium.

scenario: Dev ticks 'Enable compression' on the /api/catalogue route, but the JSON still arrives uncompressed. Caching is disabled on that route.
stem: What is the most likely reason?
options: Front Door compresses only images and fonts, not JSON
Brotli is a Premium-only feature
Front Door compresses only when caching is enabled on the route
The catalogue JSON is larger than 1 KB
explanation: In Front Door, compression is part of the route's caching settings, so it doesn't apply when caching is off. Either let the origin compress the response, which Front Door passes through, or enable caching on a public route. JSON is on the default MIME list, and files from 1 KB to 8 MB qualify on both tiers.

scenario: Lighthouse in CI scores the home page 98. Search Console says mobile Largest Contentful Paint is poor, and most complaints come from Bengaluru.
stem: What should the team do first?
options: Ignore Search Console, because Lighthouse measures exactly the same metrics more precisely
Collect field data in Application Insights, split by country
Track First Input Delay instead of Interaction to Next Paint, because it is easier to pass
Raise the Front Door cache duration for index.html to a week so it loads faster
explanation: Core Web Vitals are judged on real page loads at the 75th percentile, so send the web-vitals library's numbers to Application Insights and compare countries. Lighthouse is a lab test on a fast machine and can't show what a 4G phone in Bengaluru sees. INP replaced FID in March 2024, and caching index.html for a week brings back the blank-page problem.
